newsitem.title: ITALY: Move to delay Italy EMU entry could hurt Prodi.
newsitem.headline: Move to delay Italy EMU entry could hurt Prodi.

text.p: A reported move to delay Italy's entry into European economic and monetary union (EMU) could, if successful, undermine Prime Minister Romano Prodi's campaign to force through further doses of tough budgetary medicine.

A Financial Times report saying Italy will be offered a deal delaying its entry into EMU until 2000 or 2001 was met with a chorus of denials from the governments of Germany, Italy and France, and from the European Commission.

Few economists believe Italy has any chance of meeting one of the key qualifying criteria for EMU membership in 1999 -- a requirement to bring down the ratio of the public deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) to three percent by the end of 1997.

But any sign Italy is wavering in its resolve to straighten out its finances in time for the 1999 EMU launch date could hamper budgetary belt-tightening in a country which has so far shown grudging acceptance of sacrifice in the name of Europe.
Prodi and his Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi have firmly nailed their colours to the mast of joining a currency union before the end of the century.

An early compromise which allowed Italy to join a year or two after the advance party of EMU members might cut the ground from under Prodi's feet as he gears up to pile on new pressure with a raft of fresh measures to cut the public deficit.
"This is very delicate for Prodi," said Lorenzo Stanca, chief economist at Credito Italiano. "In politics you often have a good solution which is unveiled too early and then goes up in smoke."

The government is preparing measures to slice another 15 trillion lire ($9.3 billion) off the public deficit, hot on the heels of parliament's approval of a controversial 62.5 trillion lire budget package for 1997.
Economists believe Italy, together with Spain and Portugal, have much to gain from swallowing their pride and joining EMU a year or two after the founding members.

A delay would provide a breather for German Chancellor Helmut Kohl who faces a hard task selling EMU to a sceptical public -- fearful that the single currency could be destabilised if Italy joined too early -- in elections due in October 1998.
But the timing of an announcement is of crucial importance.
"Any delay must involve a precise timetable and it (the delay) must not be too long. Even Spain needs extra time," said Renzo Avesani, chief economist at Italian savings bank Cariplo.

Unless an agreement is struck this year to delay Italian entry, European Union leaders are due to meet early next year to decide which countries should be in EMU from the outset. Prodi has said he would resign if Italy is not among them.

"If a delay is anounced soon I think it will be impossible for the government to go on with the same determination as before," said a London-based economist with a major investment bank. "Logic tells me that there would be big problems for Prodi and for his government," he added.
Prodi held firm on Wednesday to his chosen course, saying that Italy was "solemnly committed" to meeting the economic conditions for EMU membership from the outset.
The Financial Times, quoting unnamed senior monetary officials, had described the deal as "a face-saving compromise designed by senior European central bankers and monetary officials".
Prodi issued a statement rejecting such reports as false, unjustified and unfounded. "They do nothing but generate uncertainty among Italians and on financial markets," he said.
